Around half housing investors expected to pay more tax under reforms
The independent economic think tank e61 has estimated that only 53% of housing investors will pay more tax under the Federal Government's housing tax reforms and 43% will pay less.

The reforms passed in June replace the 50% capital gains tax (CGT) discount with an inflation deduction, introduce a minimum 30% capital gains tax rate, and delay when investors can deduct negative gearing losses until sale.

E61's analysis of 920,000 housing investments between 2008 and 2025 estimates that capital gains tax changes would have benefited the majority of investors, lowering CGT for 54% of investments and increasing it for 42%.
On the negative gearing side of the ledger, e61 says the changes pull in the other direction, lowering rental income tax for 28% of investors and increasing it for 49%.

e61 Institute Senior Research Economist Elyse Dwyer says while only a narrow majority of investors would pay more tax overall, the research concludes that government tax revenue would rise noticeably, driven by the highest-performing investments.
"The new way of taxing CGT is likely to raise more revenue for the budget bottom line, mainly coming from high-return investments," Ms Dwyer said
"It ties the tax bill more closely to the actual size of an investor's gain, so small and negative returns are taxed more lightly, and large real gains are taxed more heavily.
"That also brings down the overall riskiness of housing as an investment, because large positive and large negative returns get pulled closer to the middle."
The e61 analysis found that investors with high leverage, or with little other taxable income such as retirees, are the most likely to pay more tax under the changes.

While e61 is a self-described non-partisan tank driven by ex-Treasury and RBA staffers, as well as and university researchers, it should be noted that Labor MP and Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton is a co-founder.
Dr Charlton resigned his directorship at e61 on entering parliament.
Key Event
Aussie dollar flat despite firmer US dollar rise
While the US dollar rose against most of its trading partners overnight, the Aussie dollar remained relatively flat.
Here's more from the CBA's FX strategy team's morning note:
AUD/USD traded in a range around 0.7110. AUD has found some support from growing expectations of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike at next week's meeting.
Last night, RBA board member Iain Ross said the RBA's inflation targeting framework reduces the risk of a wage price spiral.
Meanwhile, RBA governor Bullock yesterday emphasised concerns about inflation expectations becoming embedded and described the unemployment rate as 'a bit tight'.
Given the inflation backdrop and recent communication, we expect the RBA to flag next week that it remains willing to raise the cash rate again if needed.
Working the other way, a broadly firmer USD and hawkish Fed commentary capped AUD/USD upside overnight.
Key Event
Saudi Arabia restarts East-West Pipeline
Saudi Arabia has restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu immediately, Reuters reported overnight.
The resumption of supplies helped to drive selling on global oil markets. Benchmark Brent crude fell by more than $2 a barrel towards $97, its lowest since September 8
Drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut the pipeline on September 13, halting crude loadings at the kingdom's Yanbu port.

Since disruption to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israeli war on Iran, OPEC's leading oil exporter has been using the pipeline to reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to Yanbu.
The pipeline was pumping at a low rate after its restart, two of the sources said.
State oil firm Saudi Aramco was seeking to increase the pumping rate to 4 million barrels per day, one of them said, without saying when this could be achieved.
Reuters is reporting the first cargo would be bound for China.
Traders were getting ready for Saudi oil loadings by moving tankers to Egypt's Mediterranean Port Said for ship-to-ship transfers and also to Sidi Kerir, another two trading sources said.

Oil prices have also dropped this week after Iran said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and because Saudi Arabia has loaded more ships at its Ras Tanura port, raising expectations of increased exports through the Strait.

Key Event
Nasdaq closes at record high in mixed Wall Street session, ASX set for modest gain
Wall Street had a mixed session overnight with the broader market essentially flat, while the tech-centric Nasdaq pushed higher into record territory and the blue-chip Dow slipped again.
• S&P 500: flat
• Nasdaq: +0.5%
While the S&P 500 hovers just below its record high, the Nasdaq again outpaced other sectors supported by Micron Technology and other AI stocks.
The success of the AI assistant, called Muse, has fuelled gains for AI-related chip stocks in recent days.
Yet some worried it could compete with retailers, online brokerages and other consumer companies. Amazon AMZN.O on Monday blocked the agent from shopping on its platform.

"There are a lot of tech stocks that are down today on Muse-related fears of one sort or another," Argent Capital Management portfolio Jed Ellerbroek told Reuters."People fear that Muse will be used to manage your insurance relationships, book your travel and search for stuff to buy."

European stocks edged higher, with the pan-European Eurostoxx 600 gaining 0.1% after posting its biggest daily gain in more than two months on Monday.
The ASX looks like joining in the rally with futures trading pointing to a modest 0.2% gain on opening.
Oil prices continued to ease on the back of an increasing flow of Saudi crude, with the restart of the East-West pipeline and ship movements through the Strait of Hormuz.
However, those losses were pared somewhat when US President Donald Trump said he could "annihilate" Iran if there was no peace deal.
